title: Bash Script 1 — Variables, Arguments, Conditions
lead: Write your first Bash script, make it executable, and work with variables, arguments, exit codes and conditions.
objectives: You write a script with a shebang, make it executable with chmod +x and start it with ./script.sh.
You assign variables and know the difference between single and double quotes, read, $(command) and $(( )).
You read arguments with $1, $# and "$@" and check exit codes with $? and exit.
You make decisions with if/elif/else, [[ ]] and test, and you use set -euo pipefail as a safety net.

sections.title: The first script: shebang and execute permission
body: A script is a text file with commands. The first line, the **shebang** `#!/bin/bash`, tells the system which interpreter runs the file. Without the **execute bit** the file cannot be started directly: `./hello.sh` then gives *Permission denied*.

`./` means 'the file in this folder'. Linux does not search the current folder for commands, so `hello.sh` alone gives *command not found*. In this module you create scripts with `printf` (or a heredoc on your VM) so you can see exactly what is in the file.

commands.what: The shebang: first line of the file, names the interpreter.
commands.where: At the top of every Bash script.
commands.why: The script runs with Bash and not with another shell such as sh.

commands.what: Sets the execute bit on a file.
commands.where: Once after you create a script.
commands.why: Without it `./script.sh` fails with Permission denied.

commands.what: Runs an executable script by path.
commands.where: When you start your own scripts.
commands.why: The path (`./` or full path) tells the shell where the file is.

commands.what: Runs a script with Bash directly, no execute bit needed.
commands.where: For quick tests and on volumes mounted noexec.
commands.why: Handy for debugging; the shebang is ignored.

sections.tip: Put your own scripts in `~/bin`. On Ubuntu and Rocky this folder is added to `PATH` at login once it exists, so you can start them by name.
sections.warn: Never run a script you downloaded or do not understand. Read it first with `cat script.sh`. Be especially careful with `curl ... | bash` and with `sudo` on a first attempt.

sections.title: Variables, quoting and arithmetic
body: A variable is set with `NAME=value` — **no spaces around `=`**. You read it with `$NAME`. `NAME = value` does not work: Bash thinks `NAME` is a command.
**Double quotes** `"..."` expand variables, **single quotes** `'...'` do not: `echo '$HOME'` prints the text `$HOME`. Always quote variables (`"$NAME"`) so file names with spaces stay one word.
`$(command)` inserts the output of a command, `$(( ))` calculates integers, `read` asks the user for input (VM only).

commands.what: Sets a variable (no spaces around the equals sign).
commands.where: At the top of a script for settings and paths.
commands.why: You change a value in one place instead of ten.

commands.what: Double quotes expand the variable, single quotes keep the text.
commands.where: In every command that uses variables.
commands.why: Quoting protects against spaces and glob characters in values.

commands.what: Reads a line of input into a variable.
commands.where: In interactive scripts that ask questions.
commands.why: `-r` keeps backslashes, `-p` shows a prompt.

commands.what: Replaces itself with the output of the command.
commands.where: To store output in a variable or use it in text.
commands.why: Lets scripts react to system state.

commands.what: Integer arithmetic.
commands.where: Counters, sizes, simple calculations.
commands.why: Bash has no decimals; for those use `bc`.

sections.tip: A default value is written `${NAME:-default}`: it is used when `NAME` is empty or unset.

sections.title: Arguments and exit codes
body: A script receives arguments: `$0` is the script name, `$1`, `$2`, ... are the arguments, `$#` is their number and `"$@"` is the list of all of them, each kept as one word. Quote `"$@"`, otherwise `my file` becomes two words.

Every command ends with an **exit code**: `0` means success, anything else means failure. `$?` holds the code of the last command. In a script you end with `exit 0` or `exit 1`. The simulator cannot run arguments in scripts reliably, so the real runs are in the VM section.

commands.what: Script name and the first arguments.
commands.where: When the script needs input from the caller.
commands.why: One script works for many files or names.

commands.what: Number of arguments and the list of all arguments.
commands.where: To check the count or loop over arguments.
commands.why: `"$@"` keeps every argument intact, even with spaces.

commands.what: First argument, or `guest` if none was given.
commands.where: For optional arguments.
commands.why: The script does not break when the argument is missing.

commands.what: `$?` is the last exit code, `exit N` ends a script with code N.
commands.where: After commands you want to check, and at the end of scripts.
commands.why: Other scripts, cron and CI decide based on this code.

sections.tip: `grep` returns 1 when nothing matches. That is not an error in the program, just a 'no' answer: `grep carol ~/users.txt; echo $?` prints `1`.

sections.title: Conditions: if, elif, else
body: `if` runs a command and looks at its exit code. The command is usually `[ ... ]` (the same as `test`) or Bash's `[[ ... ]]`. Spaces inside the brackets are required: `[ -f "$1" ]`.

Useful tests: `-f` regular file, `-d` directory, `-x` executable, `-z` string is empty, `-n` string is not empty. For numbers use `-eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge`, for text `==` and `!=`. `[[ ]]` is safer than `[ ]` (no word splitting) but exists only in Bash, not in plain `sh`.
Short forms: `cmd1 && cmd2` runs the second only on success, `cmd1 || cmd2` only on failure.

commands.what: Runs different commands depending on a test.
commands.where: Whenever a script must decide.
commands.why: Scripts react to input and state instead of running blindly.
commands.example: if [ -f "$1" ]; then echo exists; else echo missing; fi

commands.what: Tests files, strings and numbers; the result is the exit code.
commands.where: In the condition of `if`, or alone with `&&` / `||`.
commands.why: The portable form that works in every shell.

commands.what: Bash conditions with patterns and `&&` / `||` inside.
commands.where: In scripts with `#!/bin/bash`.
commands.why: Fewer quoting traps than `[ ]`.

commands.what: Chains commands by success or failure.
commands.where: For short checks on one line.
commands.why: Quick alternative to a full `if`.

sections.tip: Check first, act second: `[ -f "$1" ] || { echo "no such file"; exit 1; }` stops early with a clear message.

sections.title: Safe scripts: set -euo pipefail and debugging
body: By default Bash **continues after errors**. The line `set -euo pipefail` at the top changes that: `-e` stops at the first failing command, `-u` treats an unset variable as an error, `-o pipefail` makes a pipe fail if any part fails.

To debug use `bash -n script.sh` (syntax check only) and `bash -x script.sh` (prints every command with a `+` before running it). `shellcheck` finds typical mistakes before you run the script. Install it with `sudo apt install shellcheck` on Debian/Ubuntu or `sudo dnf install epel-release && sudo dnf install ShellCheck` on RHEL/Rocky.

On hardened systems a script can fail although `chmod +x` was done: the folder may be mounted `noexec`, or SELinux (RHEL/Rocky) / AppArmor (Ubuntu) may block it when a service starts it. Then use `bash script.sh` for a test and look at the audit/journal logs.

commands.what: Strict mode: stop on errors, unset variables and failed pipes.
commands.where: Second line of almost every script.
commands.why: Errors are not silently ignored, so the script does less damage.

commands.what: `-n` checks syntax, `-x` traces each command.
commands.where: When a script misbehaves.
commands.why: You see exactly which line and which values are used.

commands.what: Static analysis of shell scripts.
commands.where: Before you share or schedule a script.
commands.why: Finds quoting bugs and typos early.

commands.what: Aborts with a message if the variable is empty or unset.
commands.where: Before destructive commands that use a variable.
commands.why: Prevents `rm` from running on the wrong path.

sections.tip: Print first, delete later: replace `rm` with `echo rm` in a test run and check the paths with your eyes.
sections.warn: Only `-e` is no guarantee: it is ignored inside conditions (`if`, `&&`, `||`). Test every script with harmless sample data first.
sections.danger: An empty variable is dangerous: `rm -rf "$DIR"/*` becomes `rm -rf /*` when `DIR` is empty. Use `set -u` and `${DIR:?}`, test in a VM and take a **snapshot** first (module 0.2).

t01.text: Create the folder for your scripts in your home directory: `mkdir ~/bin`.

t02.text: Write your first script with `printf '#!/bin/bash\necho "Hello, Linux!"\n' > ~/bin/hello.sh`.
t02.hint: `\n` is a line break; the file gets two lines. Check with `cat ~/bin/hello.sh`.

t03.hint: Look at `ls -l ~/bin/hello.sh`: the permissions now contain `x`.

t04.text: Run the script by its path: `~/bin/hello.sh`.

t05.text: Write `~/bin/vars.sh` with the lines `#!/bin/bash`, `NAME=student` and `echo "Hello $NAME"` (use `printf`), make it executable and run it.
t05.hint: Three commands: `printf ... > ~/bin/vars.sh`, `chmod +x`, then run it. Output: `Hello student`.

t06.text: Predict: what do `'$HOME'` and `"$HOME"` print? Then check with `echo '$HOME' "$HOME"`.
t06.hint: Single quotes keep the text, double quotes expand the variable.

t07.text: Predict the exit code of a search without a match. Run `grep carol ~/users.txt; echo $?`.
t07.hint: grep finds nothing in this file and answers with a non-zero code.

t08.text: Write `~/bin/check.sh` (shebang, then `if [ -f "$1" ]; then`, `echo "exists"`, `else`, `echo "missing"`, `fi`) and make it executable. The simulator cannot run `if`; you will run it in the VM.
t08.hint: Use one `printf` with `\n` between the lines, then `chmod +x`.

t09.text: Use `test` or `[ ]` twice: check that `~/notes.txt` is a file (`-f`) and that `~/Documents` is a directory (`-d`). Add `&& echo ok` to see the result.

t10.text: Predict: is `~/notes.txt` executable? Run `test -x ~/notes.txt; echo $?` and read the code.
t10.hint: Exit code 0 means true, 1 means false.

t11.text: Debug: `~/scripts/broken.sh` has no shebang and no execute permission. Fix both (keep the two existing commands in it), then run it; it must create `~/backup.done`.
t11.hint: Rewrite the file with `printf` and add `#!/bin/bash` as the first line, then `chmod +x`.

t12.text: Debug: `~/scripts/greet.sh` should print `Hello alice` but prints the text `Hello $NAME`. Find the two mistakes (space around `=`, single quotes), fix them and run the script.
t12.hint: `NAME=alice` without spaces, and `echo "Hello $NAME"` with double quotes.

t13.text: Mini project: write `~/bin/args.sh` with a shebang and three `echo` lines that use `$1`, `$#` and `"$@"`. Make it executable.
t13.hint: Example line: `echo "Count: $#"`. Use one `printf` and `\n` between the lines.

t14.text: Mini project: write `~/bin/backup.sh`: shebang, `set -euo pipefail`, `SRC="$HOME/Documents"`, `DEST="$HOME/backup"`, `mkdir -p "$DEST"` and `cp "$SRC/report.txt" "$DEST/"`. Make it executable.
t14.hint: Quote every variable. The simulator cannot run `set`, so only create the file.

t15.text: Challenge: create `~/bin/need_arg.sh`. Without an argument it prints `Usage: need_arg.sh NAME` and ends with `exit 1`; otherwise it prints `Hello, $1` and ends with `exit 0`. Make it executable.

t16.text: Challenge: create `~/bin/probe.sh` whose only command is `test -f /home/student/missing.txt`. Make it executable, run it and write its exit code with `echo $? > ~/code.txt` into `~/code.txt`.
t16.hint: A script returns the exit code of its last command. Run `echo $?` right after the script.

t17.text: Ticket: The new-hire team wants `~/bin/welcome.sh`. With a name it prints `Welcome, NAME`; without an argument it must use `guest`. Use `${1:-guest}`, add a shebang and make it executable.

t18.text: Ticket: A colleague says `~/scripts/report.sh` fails with 'Permission denied'. Fix it with the smallest change and run it; it must create `~/report.done`.
t18.hint: The file lacks the execute bit; you do not need to edit its contents.

vm.intro: On your VM (Ubuntu or Rocky) you run the scripts for real. Use only your own `~/bin` folder and harmless test data. For destructive experiments take a snapshot first (module 0.2).

v01.title: First script and execute bit
v01.text: Create the script with a heredoc, try to run it before and after `chmod +x`, and paste the output.

blocks.cmd:
mkdir -p ~/bin
cat > ~/bin/hello.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
echo "Hello, Linux!"
EOF
~/bin/hello.sh
chmod +x ~/bin/hello.sh
ls -l ~/bin/hello.sh
~/bin/hello.sh
blocks.expected:
bash: /home/student/bin/hello.sh: Permission denied
-rwxr-xr-x. 1 student student 38 Nov 12 10:00 /home/student/bin/hello.sh
Hello, Linux!

differs: On Ubuntu `ls -l` has no dot after the permissions; on Rocky there is one (SELinux context).
If the first run already works, your umask or file system gives the execute bit; that is fine.

v02.title: Variables, quoting, read and arithmetic
v02.text: Write a script that shows the quoting difference, reads a number and doubles it. Feed the number through a pipe.

blocks.cmd:
cat > ~/bin/vars.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
NAME="student"
echo 'single: $NAME'
echo "double: $NAME"
read -r -p "Number: " N
echo "Double: $((N * 2))"
echo "Year: $(date +%Y)"
EOF
chmod +x ~/bin/vars.sh
echo 21 | ~/bin/vars.sh

differs: The prompt `Number:` is not shown because input comes from a pipe; that is normal.
If you see `unbound variable` or `syntax error`, check that there are no spaces around `=`.

v03.title: Arguments with spaces
v03.text: Write a script that prints the argument count and every argument, then call it with a file name that contains a space.

blocks.cmd:
cat > ~/bin/args.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
echo "Script: $0"
echo "Count: $#"
echo "First: $1"
for item in "$@"; do
  echo "Arg: $item"
done
EOF
chmod +x ~/bin/args.sh
~/bin/args.sh "my file" bob
blocks.expected:
Script: /home/student/bin/args.sh
Count: 2
First: my file
Arg: my file
Arg: bob

differs: If `Count` is 3, you called it without quotes around `my file`.
Replace `"$@"` with `$@` and run again: `my` and `file` become separate arguments.

v04.title: if / elif / else and exit codes
v04.text: Build a small grading script with `[[ ]]`, run it with three inputs and look at exit codes of `test`.

blocks.cmd:
cat > ~/bin/grade.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
score="${1:-0}"
if [[ $score -ge 90 ]]; then
  echo "top"
elif [[ $score -ge 50 ]]; then
  echo "pass"
else
  echo "fail"
fi
EOF
chmod +x ~/bin/grade.sh
~/bin/grade.sh 95
~/bin/grade.sh 60
~/bin/grade.sh
test -f /etc/passwd; echo "rc=$?"
test -f /nonexistent; echo "rc=$?"

differs: If you get `[[: not found`, you started the script with `sh script.sh`; use `bash` or run it directly.
If every input prints `fail`, check the spaces inside `[[ ... ]]`.

v05.title: Strict mode in action
v05.text: Compare what `set -euo pipefail` does with a failing command and with an unset variable.

blocks.cmd:
cat > ~/bin/strict.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
echo "before"
false
echo "after"
EOF
chmod +x ~/bin/strict.sh
~/bin/strict.sh; echo "exit=$?"
bash -c 'set -u; echo "$UNDEFINED_VAR"'; echo "exit=$?"
blocks.expected:
before
exit=1
bash: line 1: UNDEFINED_VAR: unbound variable
exit=1

differs: `after` must not appear. If it does, check the `set` line.
The exact wording of the `unbound variable` message depends on the Bash version.

v06.title: Debugging: bash -n, bash -x, shellcheck
v06.text: Check the syntax, trace a script and install ShellCheck (choose your distribution). If the install is not possible, skip the third block and paste the first two outputs.

blocks.cmd:
# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt install -y shellcheck
# Rocky / RHEL
sudo dnf install -y epel-release && sudo dnf install -y ShellCheck
shellcheck ~/bin/vars.sh

differs: `syntax=0` means the syntax is fine; any other number means a syntax error and Bash prints the line.
If ShellCheck prints hints like SC2086, they usually point to missing quotes around a variable.

q1.explain: Single quotes prevent expansion; the text `$HOME` is printed. Only double quotes expand variables.

q2.q: What does `$#` contain inside a script?
options: The exit code of the last command
q2.explain: `$#` is the argument count; `$0` is the script name, `$?` the last exit code and `"$@"` the list of arguments.

options: Prints each command before it runs
Stops on errors, unset variables and failed parts of a pipe
q3.explain: `-e` stops on errors, `-u` on unset variables and `pipefail` on failing pipe parts. Printing commands is `-x`.

q4.q: You start `./run.sh` and the file has no execute bit. What happens?
q4.explain: Without the x bit the kernel refuses to start the file: Permission denied. Fix it with `chmod +x run.sh`.

summary: A script starts with the shebang `#!/bin/bash`, needs `chmod +x` and is started with `./script.sh`.
Variables: `NAME=value` without spaces; `"$NAME"` expands, `'$NAME'` does not. Always quote.
`$1`, `$#` and `"$@"` read arguments; `${1:-default}` sets a default.
`$?` is the last exit code (0 = success); `exit N` ends a script with a code.
`if` with `[ ]`, `[[ ]]` or `test` decides; `-f -d -z -eq` are the most common tests.
`set -euo pipefail` plus `bash -x` and `shellcheck` make scripts safer and easier to debug.

glossary.meaning: The first line `#!/bin/bash`; names the interpreter of the script.
The x permission that allows a file to be started as a program.
A named value, set with `NAME=value` and read with `$NAME`.
Single quotes keep text literally, double quotes expand variables.
A value passed to the script: `$1`, `$2`, ...
A number returned by a command; 0 is success, everything else is failure.
A command that evaluates a condition and answers with an exit code.
`set -euo pipefail`: stop on errors, unset variables and failed pipes.
`<<'EOF'` passes several lines of text to a command, often to create a file.
